note:
ED visit. 19-year-old male.
CC: itchy rash x 2 wks, worse x 4 d

HPI: pt w/ hx atopic dermatitis since childhood, c/o flare of itchy rash on both arms, neck and behind knees. Scratching all night, poor sleep x 4 nights. Using OTC hydrocortisone 1% cream BID x 10 d w/o relief. Stress from finals this month. Crusting on R forearm x 3 d w/ mild tenderness. Pt asking for something stronger and something to help him sleep.
Denies fever, chills. No eye pain, no vision change. No facial swelling. No SOB, no wheezing. No new soaps, detergents or meds. No cold sore exposure.

PMH: atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, mild intermittent asthma
Meds: cetirizine 10 mg daily, albuterol inhaler 2 puffs PRN
NKDA. No tobacco, occasional EtOH.

VS: Temp 98.9 F, HR 82, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% RA

PE: NAD, A&Ox3. Dry scaly erythematous plaques w/ excoriations in antecubital and popliteal fossae and posterior neck. Lichenification at antecubital fossae. Honey-colored crusting w/ few pustules R forearm, approx 3 cm. No vesicles, no punched-out erosions. No facial involvement. No cervical LAD. Lungs CTAB, no wheezes.

ED course: wound swab cx sent from R forearm. CBC: WBC 9.1.

Dx: AD flare w/ secondary impetiginization R forearm. No s/s eczema herpeticum.

Tx + dispo:
- stop hydrocortisone 1% cream (too weak)
- start triamcinolone 0.1% ointment BID to body x 2 wks, not on face or groin
- start cephalexin 500 mg QID x 7 d
- start hydroxyzine 25 mg qHS PRN itch, no driving after dose
- cont cetirizine 10 mg daily
- petrolatum emollient BID, short lukewarm showers
- derm referral 1-2 wks, PCP f/u
- RTED if fever, spreading redness, painful clustered blisters, eye sx
- pt verbalized understanding, d/c home
summary: A 19-year-old male with atopic dermatitis presented to the emergency department with a 2-week itchy rash that worsened over 4 days, with poor sleep and crusting on the right forearm despite hydrocortisone 1% cream. He denied fever, chills, eye pain, and wheezing, and vitals were normal. Examination showed excoriated erythematous plaques with honey-colored crusting and a few pustules on the right forearm, and WBC was 9.1. The assessment was an atopic dermatitis flare with secondary impetiginization and no signs of eczema herpeticum. Hydrocortisone was stopped, triamcinolone, cephalexin, and hydroxyzine were started, and dermatology referral and return precautions were given.

soap.subjective: 19-year-old male with childhood atopic dermatitis, allergic rhinitis, and mild intermittent asthma presents with an itchy rash on both arms, neck, and behind the knees for 2 weeks, worse over 4 days, with scratching all night and poor sleep. Denies fever, chills, eye pain, vision change, facial swelling, SOB, wheezing, new soaps or medications, and cold sore exposure. Takes cetirizine 10 mg daily and albuterol inhaler PRN. NKDA. No tobacco, occasional alcohol.
soap.objective: Temp 98.9 F, HR 82, BP 122/74, RR 16, SpO2 99% on room air. NAD, A&Ox3. Dry scaly erythematous plaques with excoriations in the antecubital and popliteal fossae and posterior neck, with lichenification at the antecubital fossae. Honey-colored crusting with a few pustules on the right forearm, about 3 cm. No vesicles, punched-out erosions, facial involvement, or cervical LAD. Lungs CTAB without wheezes. Wound swab culture sent from the right forearm. WBC 9.1.
soap.assessment: Atopic dermatitis flare with secondary impetiginization of the right forearm. No signs or symptoms of eczema herpeticum.
plan: Stop hydrocortisone 1% cream because it is too weak
Start triamcinolone 0.1% ointment BID to the body for 2 weeks, not on the face or groin
Start cephalexin 500 mg QID for 7 days
Start hydroxyzine 25 mg qHS PRN itch, with no driving after the dose
Continue cetirizine 10 mg daily
Petrolatum emollient BID and short lukewarm showers
Dermatology referral in 1-2 weeks and PCP follow-up
Return to the ED for fever, spreading redness, painful clustered blisters, or eye symptoms

note:
39-year-old male, hospital ward, HD2
Admitted for RLE cellulitis

Overnight: no acute events. Low-grade temp 99.4 F at 0400. Pain 5/10 R shin, better w/ acetaminophen. CIWA scores 4, 6, 5 overnight, no lorazepam needed. Slept ok.

Hx: pt drinks approx 8-10 beers daily x several yrs, last drink ~ 2 d prior to admission. Scratched R shin on a fence ~ 5 d ago, then redness, warmth, swelling spread up leg. Seen in ED, started on vancomycin IV, admitted.
Denies fevers/chills at home, no CP, no SOB, no N/V, no tremor, no hallucinations, no hx of withdrawal seizures. No hx of DVT. No IVDU. No purulent drainage.

PMH: alcohol use disorder, HTN (not on tx), GERD
Meds: omeprazole 20 mg daily, thiamine 100 mg daily, folic acid 1 mg daily, acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN, lorazepam 1 mg PO PRN per CIWA
NKDA

VS: Temp 99.4 F, HR 96, BP 142/88, RR 18, SpO2 97% RA
PE: mildly anxious, no tremor. R shin w/ erythema ~ 12 x 10 cm, warm, tender, mild edema, borders marked w/ skin marker. No fluctuance, no crepitus, no purulence. Calf soft, nontender. Heart RRR. Lungs CTAB. Abd soft, mild hepatomegaly, no ascites. A&Ox3.

Labs: WBC 13.2 (down from 15.1), Cr 0.8, AST 78, ALT 52, Hgb 13.8, plt 168, lactate 1.2. Blood cx x2 NGTD. LE venous duplex neg for DVT.

A/P by problem:
1. RLE cellulitis, nonpurulent, improving: stop vancomycin, start cefazolin 2 g IV q8h since blood cx neg and no MRSA risk factors. Keep marking borders, elevate leg. Acetaminophen 650 mg q6h PRN, max 3 g/day given liver. No NSAIDs. Plan PO cephalexin 500 mg QID once erythema clearly receding, likely 1-2 d, total 7-10 d.
2. Alcohol use disorder, last drink 2 d ago: CIWA q4h, lorazepam 1 mg PO PRN per CIWA, cont thiamine 100 mg daily and folic acid 1 mg daily. Addiction medicine consult. Counseled on cutting down.
3. Mild transaminase elevation, likely alcohol-related: repeat LFTs in AM.
4. HTN, untreated, BP 142/88: monitor, PCP f/u after d/c, no new agent while in withdrawal window.
5. DVT ppx: enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily.
Dispo: expected d/c 1-2 d.

He had a low-grade temperature and no acute events overnight, with erythema about 12 x 10 cm and WBC 13.2 down from 15.1, negative blood cultures so far, and a negative venous duplex. Vancomycin was stopped and cefazolin started, with a planned switch to oral cephalexin. Alcohol withdrawal is monitored with CIWA, thiamine and folic acid continue, addiction medicine is consulted, and mild transaminase elevation will be rechecked.

Expected discharge in 1-2 days

note:
Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 58-year-old male here for your glaucoma follow-up. It has been about eight months since your last visit, right?
Patient: Yes, and I'm sorry about that. The bus line I used to take to the clinic was cut, and I don't have anyone who can drive me.
Doctor: That's frustrating, and I'm glad you made it today. How have your eyes been?
Patient: About the same. No eye pain, no redness, and my vision seems okay.
Doctor: Any halos around lights, or trouble seeing off to the sides?
Patient: No halos, and no trouble with my side vision.
Doctor: Are you still using the latanoprost drop?
Patient: Yes, one drop in each eye at bedtime. I've only missed it a couple of times.
Doctor: Good. Any side effects, like burning or stinging?
Patient: No burning. My eyelashes look a little longer, that's all.
Doctor: That's a common and harmless effect. Let me check the pressures. Your eye pressure is 17 in the right eye and 18 in the left, which is right where we want it. The optic nerves look stable compared with your last visit, and the visual field test we did today shows no new loss.
Patient: That's good news.
Doctor: It is. So the diagnosis is primary open-angle glaucoma, stable on latanoprost. Continue the drop every night. Since getting here is hard for you, I'll schedule your next visit in four months, and our social worker will help you set up a medical transport ride so you don't miss it. I'm also ordering an OCT scan of the optic nerve for that visit.
Patient: Thank you. That would help a lot.
summary: A 58-year-old male returned for primary open-angle glaucoma follow-up after an eight-month gap caused by transportation barriers. He denied eye pain, redness, halos, and burning, and reported using latanoprost nightly with only a couple of missed doses. Eye pressures were 17 in the right eye and 18 in the left, the optic nerves looked stable, and the visual field test showed no new loss. The glaucoma is stable, so latanoprost continues, an OCT scan is ordered, and the next visit is in four months with social work arranging medical transport.

soap.objective: Eye pressure 17 in the right eye and 18 in the left. Optic nerves look stable compared with the last visit. Visual field test today shows no new loss.
soap.assessment: Primary open-angle glaucoma, stable on latanoprost.
plan: Continue latanoprost every night
Schedule the next visit in four months
Social worker to help arrange medical transport
Order an OCT scan of the optic nerve for the next visit

note:
Orthopedic surgery progress note, postoperative day 1. The patient is a 60-year-old female with end-stage right knee osteoarthritis who underwent an uncomplicated right total knee arthroplasty yesterday under spinal anesthesia.

Overnight she had no acute events. Pain is controlled at 4 out of 10 at rest and 6 out of 10 with physical therapy, and she is using oxycodone 5 mg about every 6 hours as needed. IV hydromorphone was discontinued this morning as her pain improved. She is tolerating a regular diet and voiding without difficulty. She worked with physical therapy yesterday afternoon and walked 30 feet with a walker.

On review of her history, she disclosed that she stopped taking celecoxib 200 mg daily about two months ago because the copay was too expensive for her. Since then she has been using over-the-counter ibuprofen 400 mg on and off, and she sometimes skips doses of her blood pressure medication, amlodipine 5 mg daily, to make her prescriptions last longer. She denies chest pain, shortness of breath, calf pain, nausea, vomiting, or numbness and tingling in the right foot.

Vitals this morning: temperature 99.1 F, heart rate 84, blood pressure 134/78, respiratory rate 16, oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. The right knee dressing is clean, dry, and intact with mild expected swelling and some bruising. There is no erythema or drainage. Her calves are soft and nontender, distal pulses are 2+, and sensation is intact to light touch. She can perform a straight leg raise and flex the knee to 70 degrees. Labs this morning show hemoglobin 10.2 g/dL, down from 12.6 g/dL before surgery, and creatinine 0.8 mg/dL.

Overall she is doing well on postoperative day 1 after right total knee arthroplasty for knee osteoarthritis, with expected postoperative anemia that does not need transfusion, and a history of hypertension that is currently controlled. We will continue multimodal analgesia with scheduled acetaminophen 1000 mg every 8 hours, oxycodone 5 mg every 6 hours as needed, and ice and elevation. She will also start enoxaparin 40 mg subcutaneously daily for DVT prophylaxis. Amlodipine 5 mg daily will be resumed, and she was told to stop the over-the-counter ibuprofen and not to restart celecoxib for now. Physical therapy will see her twice a day, and we will repeat the CBC in the morning. Case management and social work are consulted today to look into medication affordability and patient assistance programs, and we will discuss a low-cost generic option for her long-term arthritis pain before discharge.

note: This is a dictation for an inpatient eye evaluation on hospital day 3. The patient is a 64-year-old male admitted three days ago with community-acquired pneumonia, who also has type 2 diabetes, and who developed redness and yellow discharge in the left eye yesterday morning, correction, it was the right eye, and today the left eye has become red and watery as well. He woke up this morning with both eyelids crusted shut and says the eyes feel gritty. He denies eye pain, sensitivity to light, blurred vision, or any change in his vision, and he does not wear contact lenses. He also denies sore throat, ear pain, and nasal congestion. He has a cough from the pneumonia that is slowly improving. Home medications include metformin 1000 mg twice a day, which has been held since admission, and several over-the-counter supplements, namely ginkgo biloba 120 mg twice a day, fish oil 1000 mg daily, and biotin 5000 mcg daily. For the past two days he has also been using an over-the-counter naphazoline redness relief drop several times a day, which he brought from home. In the hospital he is receiving ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg daily for the pneumonia. He has no known drug allergies. Vital signs today are temperature 99.0, heart rate 80, blood pressure 136/80, respiratory rate 18, and oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. White count this morning is 11.4, down from 14.2 on admission, and glucose is 148. On exam visual acuity is 20/30 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left with his glasses, pupils are equal and reactive, and extraocular movements are full. There is diffuse conjunctival injection in both eyes, worse on the right, with mucopurulent discharge and crusting along the lid margins. The corneas are clear, fluorescein staining shows no ulcer or abrasion, the anterior chamber is quiet, and there is no preauricular lymphadenopathy. The oropharynx is clear and the ear canals and tympanic membranes look normal. My impression is acute bacterial conjunctivitis, worse in the right eye than the left, in a patient with community-acquired pneumonia and type 2 diabetes. For the plan, start moxifloxacin 0.5 percent ophthalmic solution one drop in both eyes three times daily for seven days. Stop the naphazoline drops because they can worsen redness. Hold the ginkgo biloba while he is in the hospital because of bleeding risk, and hold the biotin because it can interfere with some lab assays. Use warm compresses, strict hand hygiene, contact precautions, and no sharing of towels. A conjunctival culture is not needed now but will be sent if there is no improvement in 48 hours. Continue the ceftriaxone and azithromycin per the primary team. Ophthalmology clinic follow-up in one week, and he should call right away for eye pain, light sensitivity, or loss of vision.
summary: A 64-year-old male hospitalized on day 3 for community-acquired pneumonia and type 2 diabetes developed redness and yellow discharge in the right eye, then the left, with eyelids crusted shut and a gritty feeling. He denied eye pain, light sensitivity, and vision change, and he had been using over-the-counter naphazoline drops plus ginkgo biloba, fish oil, and biotin supplements. Exam showed diffuse conjunctival injection with mucopurulent discharge, worse on the right, a clear cornea without fluorescein uptake, and WBC of 11.4. The impression was acute bacterial conjunctivitis, so moxifloxacin drops were started, naphazoline was stopped, ginkgo and biotin were held, and ophthalmology follow-up was arranged.

soap.subjective: 64-year-old male on hospital day 3 for community-acquired pneumonia with type 2 diabetes. Redness and yellow discharge in the right eye since yesterday morning, now with a red and watery left eye, eyelids crusted shut this morning, and gritty-feeling eyes. Denies eye pain, sensitivity to light, blurred vision, any change in vision, sore throat, ear pain, and nasal congestion. Does not wear contact lenses. Cough from the pneumonia is slowly improving. Home medications are metformin 1000 mg twice a day (held since admission), ginkgo biloba 120 mg twice a day, fish oil 1000 mg daily, and biotin 5000 mcg daily; he has used over-the-counter naphazoline drops several times a day for 2 days. Receiving ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily and azithromycin 500 mg daily. No known drug allergies.
soap.objective: Temperature 99.0, heart rate 80, blood pressure 136/80, respiratory rate 18, oxygen saturation 95 percent on room air. WBC 11.4 (14.2 on admission), glucose 148. Visual acuity 20/30 right and 20/25 left with glasses, pupils equal and reactive, extraocular movements full. Diffuse conjunctival injection in both eyes, worse on the right, with mucopurulent discharge and lid margin crusting. Corneas clear, fluorescein staining shows no ulcer or abrasion, anterior chamber quiet, no preauricular lymphadenopathy. Oropharynx clear, ear canals and tympanic membranes normal.
soap.assessment: Acute bacterial conjunctivitis, worse in the right eye than the left, in a patient with community-acquired pneumonia and type 2 diabetes.
plan: Start moxifloxacin 0.5 percent ophthalmic solution one drop in both eyes three times daily for seven days
Stop the naphazoline drops because they can worsen redness
Hold ginkgo biloba while in the hospital because of bleeding risk and hold biotin because it can interfere with lab assays
Warm compresses, strict hand hygiene, contact precautions, and no sharing of towels
Send a conjunctival culture if there is no improvement in 48 hours
Continue ceftriaxone and azithromycin per the primary team
Ophthalmology clinic follow-up in one week, call right away for eye pain, light sensitivity, or loss of vision

note:
Doctor: Hi, good to see you again. You're a 59-year-old female here for your kidney follow-up, correct?
Patient: Yes. I saw my lab results online and the kidney number was lower than before. I got scared.
Doctor: Let's go over it. Your creatinine is 1.7 and your eGFR is 33, which is stage 3b chronic kidney disease. Six months ago the eGFR was 35, so it is essentially stable. Any swelling in your legs, foamy urine, or changes in how much you urinate?
Patient: No swelling, no foamy urine, and I urinate normally.
Doctor: Any nausea, itching, or loss of appetite?
Patient: No nausea, no itching, and my appetite is fine.
Doctor: Good. Are you still taking the losartan for your high blood pressure?
Patient: Yes, 50 mg every morning. I don't take any ibuprofen or those pain pills, like you told me.
Doctor: Great. And I see you're still smoking.
Patient: About half a pack a day. I've tried quitting but it's hard.
Doctor: Smoking speeds up kidney damage and raises your heart risk, so quitting is the best thing you can do for your kidneys right now. Would you be willing to try a nicotine patch?
Patient: Yes, I'd try that.
Doctor: Okay. Your blood pressure today is 134/80 and your heart rate is 76. Your heart and lungs sound normal and there's no swelling in your legs. Your urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio was 85 mg/g, which is mildly elevated.
Doctor: So my impression is stage 3b chronic kidney disease, stable, with acceptable blood pressure, and ongoing tobacco use. Continue losartan 50 mg daily. I'm starting a nicotine patch, 14 mg once daily, and I'll refer you to the state quitline. We'll repeat your kidney panel and urine albumin in three months. Keep avoiding NSAIDs.
Patient: Thank you, that makes me feel better.
summary: A 59-year-old female with stage 3b chronic kidney disease and high blood pressure came for follow-up after seeing a lower kidney number online. Start a nicotine patch 14 mg once daily

Continue avoiding NSAIDs

Doctor: Good morning. I understand you're a 71-year-old male scheduled for a right knee replacement in three weeks, and your surgeon wants me to check your heart first. Is that right?
Patient: Yes, doc. My knee has been terrible for years, so I'm ready to get it done.
Doctor: Do you ever get chest pain or pressure, either at rest or when you're active?
Patient: No chest pain at all.
Doctor: Shortness of breath, palpitations, or fainting spells?
Patient: None of those.
Doctor: How active are you? Can you climb a couple of flights of stairs without stopping?
Patient: I can climb two flights, a little slow because of the knee, but I don't get winded. I also walk the dog a mile every morning.
Doctor: That's good functional capacity. Any history of heart attack, stroke, heart failure, diabetes, or kidney problems?
Patient: No, just high blood pressure.
Doctor: What do you take for it?
Patient: Amlodipine, 5 mg once a day.
Doctor: Any problems with anesthesia in the past?
Patient: I had a hernia repair years ago and it went fine.
Doctor: Good. Your blood pressure today is 128/76 and your heart rate is 70 and regular. Your heart sounds are normal with no murmur, your lungs are clear, and there's no swelling in your ankles. Your ECG shows normal sinus rhythm with no signs of an old heart attack or ischemia.
Doctor: So my impression is that you're at low risk for cardiac complications with this surgery. You have good functional capacity, no heart symptoms, and a normal ECG, so you don't need a stress test or an echocardiogram. Continue amlodipine 5 mg daily, including the morning of surgery with a sip of water. I'll send a note to your surgeon, and we don't need to see you again unless something changes.
Patient: That's a relief. Thank you.
summary: A 71-year-old male with hypertension was seen for a cardiac risk assessment before a right knee replacement planned in three weeks. He denied chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, and fainting, and he can climb two flights of stairs and walk a mile daily. Blood pressure was 128/76, the heart and lung exam was normal, and the ECG showed normal sinus rhythm without ischemia. He was judged low risk for cardiac complications, so no stress test or echocardiogram is needed, amlodipine continues including the morning of surgery, and a note will go to the surgeon.

note:
Doctor: Hello, I'm glad you both could come in. So you're a 71-year-old female, and your daughter came along because of some memory trouble?
Family member: Yes. Over the past year Mom keeps repeating the same questions, and last week she left the stove on twice.
Patient: I think everyone is making a fuss. I just misplace things, like my keys and my glasses.
Doctor: Has this been getting worse?
Family member: It was subtle at first, but it is clearly worse in the last three months. She forgot a doctor's appointment and she's been missing words.
Patient: Words are on the tip of my tongue sometimes.
Doctor: Any trouble finding your way around, like getting lost while driving or walking?
Patient: No, I still drive to the store with no problem.
Doctor: Any headaches, falls, weakness on one side, or hallucinations?
Patient: No headaches, no falls, no weakness, and nothing like hallucinations.
Doctor: How is your mood? Do you feel depressed?
Patient: I'm fine, not depressed. I do have trouble falling asleep, so I take diphenhydramine 25 mg every night.
Doctor: What other medicines do you take, and do you have any allergies?
Patient: Lisinopril 10 mg daily for my blood pressure and levothyroxine 75 mcg daily for my thyroid. I'm allergic to sulfa drugs, I get a rash and my face swells.
Doctor: Thank you, I've noted the sulfa allergy. Let me examine you. Your blood pressure is 136/80 and your heart rate is 72. On the memory screening, the MoCA, you scored 21 out of 30, losing points on delayed recall and the clock drawing. Your strength, reflexes, and walking are normal, and there is no tremor.
Doctor: My impression is mild cognitive impairment, and it may be early dementia. Your hypertension and hypothyroidism are stable, but the diphenhydramine is a known cause of memory problems in older adults, so I'd like you to stop it. You can try melatonin 3 mg at bedtime for sleep instead. I'm ordering an MRI of the brain without contrast and blood tests for B12, TSH, and a metabolic panel, plus a urinalysis to rule out infection. I'm also referring you to the neurology memory clinic for neuropsychological testing. Your daughter should check on the stove, and please don't drive far until we've reviewed the results. Go to the emergency room right away for sudden confusion, weakness, or trouble speaking.
Patient: All right, I'll try that.
Family member: Thank you. We'll make sure she follows up.
summary: A 71-year-old female with a documented sulfa allergy was brought to urgent care by her daughter for a year of worsening memory problems, including repeated questions, misplaced items, missed words, and leaving the stove on. She denied headaches, falls, weakness, getting lost, hallucinations, and depression, and she takes diphenhydramine nightly for sleep. MoCA was 21 out of 30 with a normal neurologic exam. The impression was mild cognitive impairment, possibly early dementia, so diphenhydramine was stopped, melatonin started, and MRI, labs, urinalysis, and a memory clinic referral were ordered.

soap.subjective: 71-year-old female accompanied by her daughter for memory trouble. Over the past year she repeats the same questions and misplaces keys and glasses, clearly worse in the last three months, with a missed appointment, missing words, and the stove left on twice last week. Also takes lisinopril 10 mg daily and levothyroxine 75 mcg daily. Allergic to sulfa drugs with rash and facial swelling.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 136/80, heart rate 72. MoCA 21 out of 30, losing points on delayed recall and clock drawing. Strength, reflexes, and walking normal, no tremor.
soap.assessment: Mild cognitive impairment, possibly early dementia. Hypertension and hypothyroidism stable. Nightly diphenhydramine is a known contributor to memory problems.
plan: Stop diphenhydramine
Try melatonin 3 mg at bedtime for sleep
MRI of the brain without contrast
Blood tests for B12, TSH, and a metabolic panel, plus a urinalysis
Refer to the neurology memory clinic for neuropsychological testing
Daughter to check on the stove and no long-distance driving until results are reviewed
Emergency room for sudden confusion, weakness, or trouble speaking

note:
Doctor: Hi, come on in and have a seat. I see you're a 51-year-old female and this is your first time at our urgent care. What brings you in today?
Patient: My leg. Whenever I walk about a block, my right calf starts cramping and burning so badly that I have to stop. It goes away after a few minutes of rest, and then it starts again when I walk.
Doctor: How long has that been going on?
Patient: About three weeks. But I was in the hospital until a little over two weeks ago, so I wasn't walking much before that.
Doctor: I see in your discharge papers that you were admitted for a heart attack. Tell me what happened.
Patient: I had a heart attack and they put a stent in one of the arteries in my heart. I stayed five days.
Doctor: Do you have any rest pain, like leg pain when you're lying down or at night?
Patient: No, only when I walk. Nothing at rest.
Doctor: Any sores or wounds on your feet?
Patient: No sores. My right foot feels colder than the left, though.
Doctor: Any chest pain or shortness of breath since you went home?
Patient: No chest pain and no shortness of breath.
Doctor: Any bleeding or black stools? You're on two blood thinners.
Patient: No bleeding and no black stools.
Doctor: Let's go through your medications. Tell me what you take.
Patient: Aspirin 81 mg every day, clopidogrel 150 mg once a day, atorvastatin 80 mg at night, metoprolol succinate 25 mg once a day, lisinopril 5 mg once a day, and metformin 1000 mg twice a day for my diabetes. Oh, and I take ibuprofen 400 mg three or four times a day for the leg pain.
Doctor: Can you read me the clopidogrel and metoprolol bottles? I want to be sure of those doses.
Patient: Okay, hold on. I'm sorry, the clopidogrel says 75 mg, not 150. And the metoprolol succinate says 50 mg, not 25.
Doctor: Thank you, that matches your hospital records. So clopidogrel 75 mg and metoprolol succinate 50 mg, both once a day. Do you smoke?
Patient: I smoked a pack a day for about 25 years, but I quit the day I got to the hospital.
Doctor: That is the most important thing you can do for your legs, so well done. Who is at home to help you?
Patient: Nobody, I live alone. My sister lives in another state. A neighbor drove me today but I can't count on her, and I missed my cardiology follow-up last week because I had no ride.
Doctor: Thank you for telling me, we'll work on that. Let me examine you. Your blood pressure is 148/86, your heart rate is 68, and your oxygen saturation is 98 percent. Your heart is regular and your lungs are clear. The right foot is cool with mild pallor, and the capillary refill is slow at four seconds. I can't feel the pulses in the right foot, and they are faint on the left. Your calves are soft with no swelling and no tenderness, and there are no ulcers on either foot. We did an ankle-brachial index here, and it is 0.62 on the right and 0.81 on the left, which confirms reduced blood flow, worse on the right. From your hospital labs, your hemoglobin was 12.1, creatinine 0.9, hemoglobin A1c 7.8 percent, and LDL 88.
Doctor: So here is my impression. You have peripheral artery disease, which means the arteries to your legs are narrowed, and it is causing intermittent claudication in your right calf. There are no signs of critical limb ischemia, since you have no rest pain and no wounds. This is on top of your recent heart attack and stent, your type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol.
Doctor: Here is the plan. First, keep taking aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg every day and don't miss doses because of the stent, and continue atorvastatin 80 mg at night. Second, stop the ibuprofen, because with two blood thinners it raises your bleeding risk and it is hard on your kidneys. Third, your blood pressure is above goal, so I'm increasing the lisinopril from 5 mg to 10 mg once a day, and we will check a basic metabolic panel in two weeks. Fourth, I'm ordering an arterial duplex ultrasound of both legs and referring you to vascular surgery. Fifth, walk until the calf pain is moderate, rest, and repeat, for 30 minutes at least three times a week, and I'll refer you to cardiac rehab, which includes supervised exercise. Sixth, check your feet every day and wear shoes at all times. Because you live alone, I'm also asking our social worker to set up transportation for your appointments and a home health nurse to help with your pill organizer.
Patient: Okay, I'm a little overwhelmed, but I'll try. What if my leg gets worse?
Doctor: Go to the emergency room right away if you get pain in the leg at rest, if the foot turns cold, pale, or blue, if you get a sore that won't heal, or if you have chest pain. We'll also give you a written list of your medications with the changes.
Patient: Thank you, doctor.
summary: A 51-year-old female who lives alone and was hospitalized for a heart attack with a stent about two and a half weeks ago presented with right calf cramping and burning after walking about a block. She has no rest pain, sores, chest pain, or bleeding, and bottle checks corrected her clopidogrel to 75 mg and metoprolol succinate to 50 mg. The right foot was cool with pallor and absent pulses, and the ankle-brachial index was 0.62 on the right and 0.81 on the left. The diagnosis was peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication and no critical limb ischemia. Ibuprofen was stopped, lisinopril was increased to 10 mg, and duplex ultrasound, vascular surgery, cardiac rehab, and social work were arranged.

soap.subjective: 51-year-old female, hospitalized for a heart attack with a stent about two and a half weeks ago, with about three weeks of right calf cramping and burning after walking about a block that resolves with a few minutes of rest. Right foot feels colder than the left. Denies rest pain, sores, chest pain, shortness of breath, bleeding, and black stools. Takes aspirin 81 mg every day, clopidogrel 75 mg once a day (corrected from 150 mg after checking the bottle), atorvastatin 80 mg at night, metoprolol succinate 50 mg once a day (corrected from 25 mg), lisinopril 5 mg once a day, metformin 1000 mg twice a day, and ibuprofen 400 mg three or four times a day for leg pain. Smoked a pack a day for about 25 years and quit on arrival to the hospital. Lives alone with limited support, sister out of state, and missed her cardiology follow-up last week for lack of a ride.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 148/86, heart rate 68, oxygen saturation 98 percent. Heart regular, lungs clear. Right foot cool with mild pallor, capillary refill 4 seconds, no pulses felt in the right foot and faint on the left. Calves soft without swelling or tenderness, no ulcers on either foot. Ankle-brachial index 0.62 on the right and 0.81 on the left. Hospital labs: hemoglobin 12.1, creatinine 0.9, hemoglobin A1c 7.8 percent, LDL 88.
soap.assessment: Peripheral artery disease with intermittent claudication of the right calf, no signs of critical limb ischemia. Recent heart attack with stent, type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure above goal, and high cholesterol.
plan: Continue aspirin 81 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg every day without missed doses because of the stent
Continue atorvastatin 80 mg at night
Stop ibuprofen because of bleeding risk with two blood thinners and kidney effects
Increase lisinopril from 5 mg to 10 mg once a day and check a basic metabolic panel in two weeks
Order an arterial duplex ultrasound of both legs and refer to vascular surgery
Walk until calf pain is moderate, rest, and repeat for 30 minutes at least three times a week, and refer to cardiac rehab with supervised exercise
Check feet every day and wear shoes at all times
Social worker to arrange transportation and a home health nurse to help with the pill organizer
Go to the emergency room for rest pain, a cold, pale, or blue foot, a sore that won't heal, or chest pain
Give a written medication list with the changes

note:
Doctor: Good afternoon. You're an 84-year-old female here because of repeated bladder infections, correct? Tell me about them.
Patient: I've had three in the last year. Burning when I pee, going all the time, and the last one made me feel foggy and weak. My primary doctor gave me antibiotics each time.
Doctor: Do you know what the urine cultures grew?
Patient: She said it was E. coli every time.
Doctor: Are you having symptoms today?
Patient: Not today. No burning, no fever, no blood in the urine, and no back or side pain.
Doctor: Any leaking of urine or trouble emptying your bladder?
Patient: I leak a little when I cough, but I empty fine.
Doctor: What medicines are you taking?
Patient: Nitrofurantoin 50 mg every night, which I started after the second infection, and amlodipine 5 mg every morning for blood pressure. I also take cranberry capsules sometimes. I still got the last infection about two weeks ago while taking the nitrofurantoin.
Doctor: Any allergies?
Patient: No allergies.
Doctor: Do you smoke?
Patient: About five cigarettes a day. I've smoked since I was a teenager.
Doctor: Smoking raises the risk of bladder problems, including bladder cancer, so I'd like to help you cut down. Now the exam. Your blood pressure is 138/76, heart rate 74, and temperature 98.2. Your belly is soft with no tenderness over the bladder and no tenderness in the flanks. On the pelvic exam the vaginal tissues look thin and dry, which is atrophy, and there is no prolapse. A bladder scan after you urinated showed only 35 mL left, so you empty well. Your urinalysis today is clean, with no infection and no blood. Your creatinine from last month was 1.2 mg/dL.
Doctor: My impression is recurrent urinary tract infections, most likely related to vaginal atrophy after menopause, plus ongoing tobacco use. The nitrofurantoin did not prevent this last infection, and at your age and kidney function I don't want you on it long term, so I'm stopping it. I'm starting estradiol vaginal cream, 0.5 g twice a week at bedtime, which restores the tissue and reduces infections. You can keep the cranberry capsules and keep taking the amlodipine. I'm ordering an ultrasound of your kidneys and bladder. Drink plenty of water, empty your bladder regularly, and we'll talk about quitting smoking at each visit. Come back in three months.
Patient: Okay, that sounds reasonable.
summary: An 84-year-old female who smokes about five cigarettes a day was seen for three urinary tract infections in the past year, the last occurring about two weeks ago while taking nitrofurantoin prophylaxis. She has no current burning, fever, hematuria, or flank pain. Exam showed no abdominal or flank tenderness, thin and dry vaginal tissue, a post-void residual of 35 mL, and a clean urinalysis. The impression was recurrent urinary tract infections related to vaginal atrophy, with tobacco use. Nitrofurantoin was stopped, estradiol vaginal cream was started, a kidney and bladder ultrasound was ordered, and follow-up is in three months.

soap.subjective: 84-year-old female with three bladder infections in the last year, each treated with antibiotics, with E. coli on culture every time. Past infections caused burning, urinary frequency, and a foggy, weak feeling. The last infection was about two weeks ago while taking nitrofurantoin 50 mg every night. Today denies burning, fever, blood in the urine, and back or side pain. Leaks a little when she coughs but empties fine. Also takes amlodipine 5 mg every morning and cranberry capsules sometimes. No allergies. Smokes about five cigarettes a day since her teens.
soap.objective: Blood pressure 138/76, heart rate 74, temperature 98.2. Abdomen soft without tenderness over the bladder or in the flanks. Pelvic exam shows thin, dry vaginal tissue consistent with atrophy and no prolapse. Bladder scan after voiding showed 35 mL residual. Urinalysis today clean with no infection and no blood. Creatinine 1.2 mg/dL last month.
soap.assessment: Recurrent urinary tract infections, most likely related to vaginal atrophy after menopause, with ongoing tobacco use. Nitrofurantoin prophylaxis failed.
plan: Stop nitrofurantoin because it did not prevent the last infection and is not wanted long term at her age and kidney function
Start estradiol vaginal cream 0.5 g twice a week at bedtime
Continue cranberry capsules and amlodipine
Order an ultrasound of the kidneys and bladder
Drink plenty of water, empty the bladder regularly, and discuss quitting smoking at each visit
Return in three months

note:
Pulmonology clinic follow-up. This is a 31-year-old female with COPD returning for maintenance follow-up. She was diagnosed two years ago after presenting with chronic cough and exertional dyspnea, and spirometry at that time showed an FEV1 of 62 percent of predicted. She currently smokes about 10 cigarettes per day and has an approximately 12 pack-year history.

Since her last visit she has had no exacerbations, emergency visits, or hospitalizations. She reports a daily cough productive of small amounts of white sputum and mild shortness of breath when climbing two flights of stairs. She denies wheezing at night, fever, hemoptysis, chest pain, or leg swelling. She takes tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once daily and reports not missing doses, and she uses albuterol 2 puffs as needed about twice a week.

On examination, blood pressure was 118/70, heart rate 76, respiratory rate 14, and oxygen saturation 96 percent on room air. She was in no distress and speaking in full sentences. Breath sounds were slightly diminished at the bases with no wheezes or crackles, heart sounds were regular, and there was no peripheral edema. Spirometry today showed a post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 59 percent of predicted with an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.64, consistent with moderate COPD and stable compared with prior testing.

Overall she has stable moderate COPD and continues to smoke. She will continue tiotropium daily and albuterol as needed, and her inhaler technique was reviewed and is correct. Smoking cessation was discussed in detail; she is thinking about quitting and was given state quitline information. She will be referred to pulmonary rehabilitation and will return in three months, with repeat spirometry in six months.
summary: A 31-year-old female with COPD who currently smokes about 10 cigarettes per day returned for maintenance follow-up. She has had no exacerbations, emergency visits, or hospitalizations, with a daily cough, mild shortness of breath on stairs, and no wheezing at night, fever, hemoptysis, or chest pain. Oxygen saturation was 96 percent and spirometry showed a post-bronchodilator FEV1 of 59 percent of predicted, consistent with stable moderate COPD. Tiotropium and as-needed albuterol continue, smoking cessation was discussed with quitline information, and she is referred to pulmonary rehabilitation with follow-up in three months.

68-year-old female. Hospital ward, HD3. Admitted w/ RLE cellulitis after failing outpt cephalexin.

Overnight: no events. Afebrile. Pain 3/10 R lower leg. Appetite fair. Pt says leg looks better.

Hx: per pt, took cephalexin 500 mg once a day instead of QID after urgent care visit last wk, took it when she remembered, did not understand the instructions on the paper. Limited health literacy, RN screen ~ 5th grade reading level. Teach-back and picture-based instructions used today.
Denies fever, chills, CP, SOB, N/V. No new rash. No drainage. No hx of DVT.

PMH: T2DM, HTN, obesity
Home meds: metformin 1000 mg BID (held on admission), amlodipine 5 mg daily
Inpt: cefazolin 2 g IV q8h (HD1-3), insulin lispro sliding scale, clotrimazole 1% cream BID to toes (started HD2), enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily
NKDA

VS: Temp 98.4 F, HR 78, BP 136/74, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA
PE: A&Ox3, NAD. R lower leg erythema receding, border now ~ 4 cm inside marker, mild warmth, trace edema, nontender. No fluctuance, no ulcer. Interdigital maceration and scaling between R toes 3-4. DP pulses 2+.

Labs: WBC 8.9 (14.6 on adm), Cr 0.9, glucose 168 (fingersticks 140-200), A1c 8.4%. Blood cx x2 no growth at 48 h.

A/P:

summary: A 68-year-old female with limited health literacy is on hospital day 3 for right lower extremity cellulitis after failing outpatient cephalexin, which she took once a day because she did not understand the instructions. She has been afebrile with erythema receding, WBC down to 8.9 from 14.6, and negative blood cultures at 48 hours. Tinea pedis between the toes is the likely portal of entry, and her A1c is 8.4%. Cefazolin is changed to oral cephalexin, clotrimazole continues, metformin is resumed, and pharmacist and nurse teach-back with picture-based instructions is planned before discharge home tomorrow.
